chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Jamhur, from one of his companions, from Ali ibn Hadeed, who said:

I said to Abu Al-Hasan Al-Mazi (peace be upon him): 'I enter upon a group of people while they are eating, and I have already prayed Asr, and I am fasting. So they say to me, 'Break your fast.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Break, for it is superior.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a fasting person who is asked to break their fast by hosts after praying Asr?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the virtue of *ikram al-nafs* (honoring the self) and social hospitality, where breaking the fast is deemed superior to maintaining it when invited by companions. In Shia jurisprudence, this establishes that the reward for accepting a brother's invitation and breaking the fast in this specific context outweighs the reward of continuing the fast, emphasizing communal bonds over individual asceticism.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Muhammad, from Ibn Jamhour, from one of his companions, from Ali Bin Hadeed who said,

‘I said to Abu Al-Hassan Al-Maazy<sup>asws</sup> (7<sup>th</sup> Imam<sup>asws</sup>), ‘I go over to the group of people and they are eating, and Al-Asr has arrived, and I am Fasting. So they are saying, ‘Break’’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Break, for it is superior’.
en.sarwar: 5. Ali ibn Muhammad has narrated from ibn Jumhur from certain individuals of his people from Ali ibn Hadid who has said the following:

“I once asked abu al-Hassan, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, ‘I may visit a people after late afternoon prayer while I am fasting and they offer me food, saying, “discontinue your fast.’” He (the Imam) said, ‘Accept the offer; it is better.’”
